submission.natural_language_explanation: Retrospective lexical detector at layer 1: the pole fires on the current token itself (86% of the input attribution sits on it; the same word peaks the same amount to within ~0.2 of scale whatever precedes it and at any position >= 1, and no token fires at position 0) when that token is a rare, specific word - a long-tail proper name (' Scotland' 0.92, ' Stockholm' 1.83, ' Sheffield' 0.84 on its 'ffield' piece, ' Liverpool' 1.17), a rare concrete noun (' magnet' 1.47, ' flour' 1.37, ' pumpkin' 1.27, ' butter' 1.07, ' Lyon' 0.79) or the stem/fragment of a rare technical word (' adren-' 1.92, ' cytok-' 1.79, ' cortisol' 1.53, ' neuron' 1.23, ' syn-' 1.52). It sits at the GELU floor (-0.17) on high-frequency vocabulary - function words, generic nouns (' city' -0.17, ' country' -0.17, ' water' -0.14, ' school' -0.16, ' market' -0.15), abstract nouns (' method' -0.17, ' system' -0.15, ' process' -0.16, ' factor' -0.16) and famous proper names (' Paris' -0.13, ' London' -0.11, ' China' -0.06, ' America' -0.15) - and roughly 80% of even rare words stay at the floor (' valley' +0.04, ' needle' +0.04, ' stream' +0.01, ' enormous' -0.15, ' antiquated' -0.11), so this is a graded long-tail detector rather than a switch on all rare tokens; the negative pole is only GELU's dip and carries no separate content.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
I had always been the kind of person who said yes to everything. In January I agreed to lead the neighbourhood committee, in February I took on a second job at the library, and by March I was driving my sister's children to school every morning before my own shift began. I told myself that busy was good, that idle hands were a waste, that the tiredness I felt at the end of each day was simply the price of a full life.

My friends noticed before I did. They saw that I had stopped laughing at jokes, that I read the same page of a book three nights in a row, that I cancelled dinner twice and then apologised with a box of cakes nobody wanted. When my sister asked how I was sleeping, I said fine, and then admitted that I had not slept through a single night since the clocks changed.

The first sign was the headaches. They arrived each afternoon, a band of pressure behind my eyes that no amount of water or fresh air would shift. Then came the strange forgetfulness: I would stand in a room unable to remember why I had walked into it, or drive past my own street because I had been thinking about a meeting. My skin broke out, my shoulders ached, and the cold I caught in April lasted nearly five weeks.

I went to see my doctor in the middle of May. The waiting room was full of people with folders and forms, and I sat for forty minutes reading a poster about hand washing. The doctor asked a long series of questions about my week, my work, my family, and how often I woke in the night. I answered honestly for the first time in months. He listened, took my blood pressure twice, and wrote a few notes on the screen.

Then he explained what he thought was happening. The body, he said, has a system for dealing with danger, and it works well when the danger is short: the heart speeds up, the muscles tense, the mind narrows to the problem in front of it. The trouble comes when the danger never quite ends. When the phone keeps ringing and the list keeps growing and the alarm goes off at six every morning, the same system stays switched on. Over weeks and months, that constant readiness wears the body down, and one of the clearest markers of it is a hormone called cortisol, which the doctor could measure with a simple blood test.

I was not surprised by the result, though I pretended to be. The doctor did not prescribe anything dramatic. He asked me to write down three things I would stop doing, and to leave one evening a week completely empty. I found that harder than it sounds. The first week I filled the empty evening with chores, and the second week I sat on the sofa with my phone in my hand, waiting for it to be over. By the third week I had started walking to the park at the end of the street, and by the fourth I was sleeping until seven.

I still have busy weeks, and I still say yes more often than I should. But I have learned to notice the early signs, and to treat them as a message rather than a nuisance.
